lesson.title: Cleaning Up Input: The strip() Method
lesson.summary: The strip() method removes leading and trailing whitespace (or other specified characters) from a string, which is essential for cleaning up user input and file data.
lesson.body:
Text that comes from outside your program, typed by a user, read from a file, or pulled from another source, almost never arrives perfectly tidy. It often carries invisible passengers: a trailing newline character left over from reading a line from a file, a stray space someone typed before pressing enter, or leading whitespace introduced by formatting. The strip() method, another core piece of the string toolkit alongside .upper() and .lower(), exists specifically to remove that unwanted whitespace from the two ends of a string.

Calling text.strip() with no arguments returns a new string with all leading and trailing whitespace removed, including spaces, tabs, and newlines. It does not touch whitespace in the middle of the string. If text = "   hello world   \n", then text.strip() traces as follows: Python scans from the front, skipping the three leading spaces until it hits 'h', and scans from the back, skipping the newline and the three trailing spaces until it hits 'd'. The result is exactly "hello world", with the single internal space between the two words left alone.

Strip has two close relatives that trim from only one side: .lstrip() removes leading whitespace only, and .rstrip() removes trailing whitespace only. All three also accept an optional argument specifying which characters to strip, not just whitespace. For example, "xxhelloxx".strip("x") removes the letter 'x' from both ends, tracing the same way: it strips 'x', 'x' from the front and 'x', 'x' from the back, leaving "hello". This argument form is worth knowing, but the whitespace-stripping default is what you will reach for constantly.

The most common real use is cleaning up lines read from a file. Reading a file line by line in Python keeps the trailing newline character on each line, so a loop like this is standard practice:

with open("names.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name = line.strip()
        print(f"Hello, {name}!")

Without the .strip() call, name would still contain that trailing "\n", and printing it would produce an extra blank line or awkward spacing you did not intend. Because strings are immutable, line.strip() produces a new cleaned string rather than editing line, which is why the code assigns the result to name.

Get in the habit of stripping any text you did not generate yourself before you compare it, store it, or display it. A single unstripped space is invisible to the eye but very visible to an equality check, and tracking down that kind of bug without knowing about strip() can burn a surprising amount of time.

A second common scenario combines stripping with the case-normalization from Upper and Lower Methods. Suppose a user is asked to confirm an action and types " Yes " with extra spaces by accident. Checking answer == "yes" fails twice over, once for the case mismatch and once for the surrounding spaces. Chaining the methods together, answer.strip().lower() == "yes", first removes the spaces and then lowercases what remains, producing a clean "yes" ready to compare. Because each method returns a new string, you can chain any number of them one after another, and Python evaluates them left to right, feeding the result of .strip() directly into .lower().
